title: Emergent Dexterity Via Diverse Resets and Large-Scale Reinforcement Learning
one_liner: A robot learns to do complex hand tasks by training from many different starting positions instead of a single fixed one.
lead: Teaching a robot to pick and manipulate objects is hard because long sequences of moves need to explore many different ways things can go wrong. Current methods need humans to carefully design training schedules and reward signals, and even then they fail on tasks like inserting drawers or screwing in objects. This paper shows that simply starting each training trial from a randomly chosen realistic position—instead of always the same starting pose—lets the robot learn complex manipulation tasks at scale without any curriculum design or human guidance.

problem.h2: Why robots fail at complex manipulation
paras: In simulation, a robot learns by trial and error (called reinforcement learning): it tries a move, gets feedback on how close it got to the goal, and adjusts. The problem: if you always reset to the same starting position and slowly move toward harder goals, the robot's learned behavior gets stuck exploring the same tiny part of the space of possible moves. It never sees the messy variety of ways objects can get stuck, tipped, or misaligned in the real world.

Long sequences of moves (like open gripper, move to object, adjust grip, lift, rotate, insert) need the robot to have seen many different combinations of 'what went wrong so far.' A standard training run keeps resetting to one comfortable starting pose, so the robot never builds this diversity of skills. It ends up like someone who has only practiced piano in one room with one tuning—frozen when faced with variety.

callout.html: Train the robot by randomly resetting it to different realistic starting positions in each trial, forcing it to master many possible situations and not get stuck on one narrow path to success.

panels.title: 1. The problem
panels.caption: Robot trained from same starting pose learns one narrow path only.

panels.title: 2. Stuck in one valley
panels.caption: All learning nudges push toward the same narrow successful behavior.

panels.title: 3. Diverse resets introduce variety
panels.caption: Each trial starts from a different realistic position; robot must adapt constantly.

panels.title: 4. Skills emerge from variety

panels.title: 5. Scales with compute
panels.caption: Larger compute means more trials from more starting states, stronger final skills.

steps.text: Offline, sample many realistic starting positions grouped by type: near the goal, near the object, in contact with object, or far away.
Check that each reset is physically valid (no collisions, no flying objects) by stepping the simulator a few frames.
During training, pick a random reset zone and a random valid starting position within it for every trial.
A single policy (called PPO, proximal policy optimization) learns from all these diverse starting points using a fixed reward and fixed hyperparameters.
Convert the proprioceptive (joint-angle) policy into a vision-based policy and send it to the real robot with no additional training.

object.h2: What the paper moves: starting positions
paras: Instead of always resetting the robot and object to the same comfortable starting configuration, OmniReset varies the starting configuration across hundreds of hand-crafted but algorithmically valid reset zones. The shift is simple but changes everything: the learning algorithm no longer navigates one narrow ravine toward the goal; it learns to climb from many different foothills, building a richer toolkit of skills.

hidden.name: Contact and state diversity covered
paras: The paper does not measure this explicitly, but it is the core lever: how much of the space of possible robot-object contacts and relative positions has the training process actually visited? When a robot always starts from the same pose, it explores a tiny slice of these interactions. By resetting from many zones, the algorithm encounters and learns from vastly more ways the gripper can touch, push, or reorient the object.

OmniReset estimates this by organizing resets into semantic regions (reaching distance, near object, in contact, grasping) and sampling uniformly across them. The paper does not compute a diversity score, but the hypothesis is clear: more diverse starting states mean the learned policy has seen more of the interaction space and thus generalizes to real-world variation.

heat.caption: Darker zones and marked ones (with border) are interaction regions where OmniReset samples most; robot learns many contact types.

reads.html: A robot learning to tie shoelaces: if you always place the laces in the same neat tangle on the same table, it learns to tie just that tangle. Real laces come tangled a hundred different ways. OmniReset hands the robot a hundred different tangle configurations during training, so it learns the universal skill, not one specific tangle.

The paper notes that advanced exploration methods (curiosity-driven, count-based, demonstration-based) add algorithmic complexity and do not scale well to massively parallel simulation. OmniReset instead trades algorithmic complexity for simplicity and scale: more interaction variety is achieved by covering diverse starting positions, not by redesigning the learning algorithm.

mechanism.h2: Why learning from diverse starts works
paras: Standard reinforcement learning finds policies by following gradient signals (nudges in the direction that reduces error). When the robot always starts from the same position, every gradient signal points toward the same narrow solution—there is one easy path downhill. The algorithm converges fast to that path, but the resulting policy fails the moment the real world starts the robot from a different pose.

By resetting to many different starting positions, every trial launches the robot from a new location with a new relationship to the goal and objects. The gradient signals now point in many different directions. The algorithm cannot converge to a single narrow behavior; instead, it must discover general skills that work from many angles. This forces the learned policy to work from many situations, not just one. Adding more compute (more parallel trials) directly translates to covering more of the starting-position space. Covering more space drives higher final performance and breaks the typical ceiling where policies plateau trapped in a narrow local solution.

stages.s: Gradient signals pull in many directions
Skills that work from many starting states

math.words: Maximize the expected sum of rewards across many trials, where each trial starts from a randomly sampled position across diverse reset zones.
math.equation: max E[sum_t gamma^t * r_t | reset ~ Diverse Zones]
symbols: add up all rewards across the full task sequence
discount factor (0.99 typically): future rewards matter slightly less than immediate ones
reward at time step t (e.g., +1 for reaching the goal)
the starting configuration is randomly sampled from multiple pre-defined zones, not always the same pose

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose a gripper-positioning task has four reset zones, each offering 50 valid starting positions (200 total).
Trial 1: reset sampled from zone A, position 17. Robot explores moves from this new angle. Learns: 'when at this pose, rotate then lift works.'
Trial 2: reset sampled from zone C, position 3. Different situation. Learns: 'when starting from here, lift first then rotate.'
Trial 3–N: each from a random zone and position. The gradient accumulates learnings across all these starting points.
Result: one policy that has internalized strategies for reaching from A, B, C, and D, not just the one 'easy' reset. Generalization emerges from the forced diversity.

math.note: The equation shows the standard RL objective, but the key difference is that the reset (starting position) varies across trials instead of staying fixed, forcing the policy to learn multiple pathways to success.

charts.title: Standard training (fixed reset)
charts.note: Policy optimizes for the narrow range of starting positions it saw during training. It succeeds on that one reset but fails on new starting positions.

charts.title: OmniReset (diverse resets)
charts.note: Policy trained from many starting positions generalizes smoothly. Performance is slightly lower in any single zone (because it is not over-specialized) but dramatically higher on average. Most importantly, it works on the real robot where starting positions vary.

items.html: If the offline reset-generation phase does not properly validate that a starting position is stable (no objects interpenetrating, no gripper flying through space), training will spend compute on broken trials. Solution: step the simulator forward a few frames and use collision checking.

items.b: Uninformed reset zones miss key interactions.
items.html: If the human designing the reset zones guesses wrong about where the robot needs to start to learn the task, coverage remains incomplete. A drawer-insertion task might need resets where the gripper is already in light contact with the drawer; if the zones only cover reaching from far away, the robot never learns in-contact manipulation. Solution: include semantic zones for the task family (reaching, near-object, grasping, inserting).

If 90% of resets come from one zone and 10% from others, the policy will over-specialize to that zone despite having diverse resets available. The gradient signal is dominated by the common zone. Solution: sample uniformly across zones.

Carefully define semantic reset zones (far, reaching, near-object, grasping), validate each one for stability, and sample uniformly at training time. Compute scales the coverage: more trials cover more of each zone, strengthening the generalization.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple simulation of a robot arm pushing a block on a table. Set up four semantic reset zones: one where the arm starts far from the block, one where it is reachable distance away, one where it is near the block, and one where it is already in contact. Train two policies side by side: one always resets to the same 'easy' starting position, the other randomly resets across all four zones. After training, test both on a held-out set of random starting positions that neither saw during training.
demo.metric_eq: Generalization gap = (success rate on training resets) - (success rate on new resets)
demo.closing: The fixed-reset policy should show a huge generalization gap (succeeds on its one training reset, fails elsewhere); the OmniReset policy should show a small gap (mediocre performance everywhere, but consistent). Demonstrate that larger compute (more parallel environments) improves the OmniReset policy further—because more trials cover more starting positions—while the fixed-reset policy plateaus because it has already converged to its narrow solution.
